extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century political/philosophical essay discussing the character and institutions of the French nobility, clergy, history, property, and reform; aimed at evaluating social-political practices and recommending measured reforms. Not a technical rubric but contains many normative criteria embedded in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobility should possess 'virtue, honor, courage, patriotism, and loyalty' and these are desirable and praiseworthy characteristics of the noblesse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes the French nobility as largely composed of men of high spirit and a delicate sense of honor, tolerably well bred, humane, hospitable, frank in conversation, with a military tone and reasonable literary tincture. These are the qualities to be prized; reforms should not abolish such virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of inferiors
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher orders should 'comport themselves towards [inferior classes] with good-nature' and avoid physical violence and routine ill-treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Striking even the most abject person is described as 'in a manner unknown' and highly disgraceful; attacks on property or personal liberty of commons were rare under ancient law. Good-natured, familiar relations with lower ranks are presented as the appropriate behavior; instances to the contrary are exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in landlord-farmer relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Landed nobles should make agreements with farmers that are not oppressive; proportions in partnerships and rents should be equitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On observation the author could not discover oppressive agreements where landletting was by rent or in partnership; exceptions may exist but should be treated as such rather than presumed general practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aversion to universal condemnation of corporate bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate bodies (nobility, clergy, etc.) should not be collectively punished for the faults of some or for ancestral crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against punishing men for the offences of their natural ancestors or creating a 'pedigree of crimes' for corporations; collective confiscation and degradation are unjust and counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abolishing institutions' names to fix vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms should target causes of vice, not simply abolish offices or names (e.g., monarchs, priests, judges) in the hope of curing social ills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues you would not cure the evil by declaring there should be no monarchs or ministers; power in some form is necessary and remedies should be applied to the permanent causes (passions) rather than to transitory organs or titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use history to diagnose causes, not as a pretext
rubrics_metrics.description: History should teach the causes of human miseries (pride, ambition, avarice, revenge, etc.) rather than be perverted as a weapon or pretext to justify partisan plunder or vengeance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cautions that perverted history may nourish dissensions and animosities; true historical wisdom obscures little names and highlights moral quality, whereas perversion uses past offences to justify present plunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causes from pretexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that passions (pride, ambition, avarice, etc.) are the causes of political storms, and religion, laws, and prerogatives are frequently only pretexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply remedies to the enduring causes of evil (human passions) rather than to the shifting pretexts; otherwise reforms will be superficial and ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility as social ornament (moderation in reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobility is 'a graceful ornament to the civil order' and some deference to such institutions is a mark of a liberal mind; reform should be measured and preserve what gives permanence to esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author endorses reform 'very short of abolition'—degrade abuses but avoid producing voids or societal ruin. Excessive leveling that destroys institutions risks social instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration between aristocracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive separation between hereditary nobility and wealthy commons (two aristocracies) is harmful; social and military ranks should not be reserved exclusively by birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The separation (especially military reserved for family men) is cited as a principal cause of destruction of the old nobility; a permanent assembly with commons' share would correct invidious distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should be judged by present merits, not caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sweeping assertions that the clergy are monsters; evaluate clergy by their actual conduct—education, morals, observance of duties—rather than by exaggerated accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports having found many clergymen of moderate minds, decorous manners, and learning; accusations of universal clerical corruption are likely exaggerated for partisan ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware reform motivated by plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: When complaints against a body (e.g., clergy) are used to justify confiscation, suspect that profit and plunder may motivate denunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An enemy is a bad witness, a robber worse; the essay warns that declamations about clerical vices are often used to animate populace to plunder, and histories are ransacked to supply pretexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate punishment of clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscating and punishing 'all prelates' indiscriminately favors the vicious and harms the reputation of the deserving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad punitive measures reduce the clerical profession's attractiveness to sober and liberal men, replacing learned clergy with low-paid, election-driven incumbents and degrading clerical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educated and decorous clergy as ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerical officers should be educated, decorous, and attentive to duties; higher clergy often possessed learning and honor and should be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives examples of vicars-general and bishops of learning and candor, arguing that many clergy deserve respect and support rather than plunder or contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of elective clergy and electioneering
rubrics_metrics.description: Elective appointment of bishops and parish clergy will expose the Church to electioneering arts and attract men of low ambition and corrupt habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elective systems without qualification criteria invite factionalism, reduce moral and intellectual quality of clergy, and transfer control to partisan or licentious elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for prescription and property rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of prescription (long possession) is part of natural law; shaking prescription undermines security of property and civil society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscations and legislative reprobation of prescription are warned against as foundational injustices: once prescription is unset, no species of property is secure and legislative assemblies can destroy property at will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to legislative confiscation and artificial currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures should not violate property rights or force acceptance of speculative symbols (paper currency) as lawful tender to cover confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Assembly's practice of compelling acceptance of their speculative symbols is accused of subverting commerce and property; respectful parliaments treat property and constructive rights with greater care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured reform rather than wholesale abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: Faults and abuses should be removed by reform 'very short of abolition'—reform the abuses without degrading entire institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly urges correcting abuses while preserving useful institutions and virtues; degradation is distinct from just punishment and can be unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: True toleration vs contemptuous neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: True toleration does not arise from despising all opinions; genuine tolerance respects important doctrines while protecting others from persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who 'tolerate' by thinking none worthy show no real benevolence; English toleration exemplified respects religion's common principles and does not condone sacrilege or proscription of innocent men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should not be a cover to abolish religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism toward projects (labeled 'Civic Education') that aim to replace religion entirely by civic instruction and enlightened self-interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay suggests that philosophical fanatics envisage a state without religion and a civic education to substitute for religious principles — a design the author regards as dangerous and preparatory to abolishing Christianity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct targets for remedies: vices not offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply remedies to human vices (frailty to vice progression) through watchful oversight and firm hands, not by removing institutional offices themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The natural progress from frailty to vice ought to be prevented; but remedies should be focused on behavior and causes rather than eliminating necessary offices or authorities that play social functions.
